implementation_cost.claim: declared cost of the frozen run
implementation_cost.value: Co-occurrence construction is a one-time sparse pass over training sequences. Barycentres cost \(O(\sum_i |\mathcal N_i| I)\) per assignment refresh for \(I\) fixed-point iterations; the extra candidate distances and ranks cost \(O(BK)\) per assignment step for batch size \(B\) and code count \(K\), plus sorting \(O(BK\log K)\). At the frozen scale (24 steps/epoch × 3000 epochs = 72,000 steps; 24,556 training items), the extra assignment work is repeated each step if assignments are refreshed each step; cache each item’s neighbour indices and recompute only its barycentre from current representations when that item is assigned. No extra trainable parameters are required.

ideas.ablation_behavior_off: Wiring check only: set N(i)=empty, define h_ik=0 and assign by reconstruction rank; do not train this arm.
ideas.ablation_both_on: The single proposed candidate: frozen training co-occurrence, curved barycentre, candidate-to-context Poincare rank plus reconstruction rank. Train once for exactly 3000 Stage 2 epochs on four cards; no ablation, sweep, seed repetition, or early stopping.
ideas.ablation_geometry_off: Wiring check only: use Euclidean weighted mean of neighbour z_j and Euclidean distance from e_k to that mean; keep the same rank fusion; do not train this arm.
ideas.behavior_computation: Before Stage 2, for every user’s longest training sequence count each unordered pair of distinct items once (symmetric row updates); L2-normalize each nonzero per-item row. Freeze sparse neighbour IDs and weights. Use training split only.
ideas.behavior_signal: Symmetric item co-occurrence from each user's longest training sequence.
ideas.cost_estimate: At frozen scale, 24 steps/epoch × 3000 epochs = 72,000 steps, 24,556 training items total. For batch size B and K first-level codes, baseline first-level B×K reconstruction work is augmented by B×K curved distances and rank operations; context costs O(sum_i |N(i)|d) per step with sparse neighbor rows, and is recomputed for current encoder outputs. No extra model or Stage 2 run; likely a modest first-layer assignment overhead, implementation should chunk B×K to bound memory.
ideas.coupling_path: Frozen neighbours and their weights select current encoder outputs for b_i; b_i and each candidate code’s curved image jointly determine h_ik; h_ik’s rank is added to the reconstruction rank that chooses the first SID code.

ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: Worth keeping if coarse assignments shift toward codes geometrically close to observed co-consumers while retaining reconstruction fit and Stage3 test_recall@10 exceeds 0.065. Record prefix predictability, co-occurrence adjacency/coherence and SID diagnostics alongside, but do not gate on them; one frozen-protocol Stage3 evaluation decides.
ideas.hyperbolic_location: First-level code assignment; subsequent residual levels use the unchanged baseline Euclidean assignments.
ideas.hyperbolic_operator: Fixed-curvature Poincare ball with c=-1; exp_0 maps tangent encoder/code vectors into the ball, projected weighted Karcher mean computes the barycentre, and Poincare distance ranks candidate codes.
ideas.key_change: At the first residual quantizer only, select the code by summing its reconstruction-error rank and its Poincare-distance-to-cooccurrence-context rank; later RQ levels retain baseline Euclidean residual assignments. This is the single candidate’s design, not an ablation plan.
ideas.leakage_boundary: Construct rows only from the training split before Stage 2; validation/test interactions are never loaded by this operator. Encoder neighbour vectors are current representations of training items only.
ideas.motivation: The first SID token defines a broad semantic region; letting training-sequence co-consumption choose among equally plausible coarse codes may make that prefix more useful for next-item prediction without forcing uniform code use.
ideas.novelty: Unlike existing successor-context and behaviour-cohesion mechanisms, the frozen symmetric co-occurrence context participates in the actual first-layer argmin through a rank fusion with reconstruction, not a separate loss or post-hoc SID feature.
ideas.observables: First-level assignments and their gradients/selected-code updates change when the training graph or curvature switch changes; record code frequencies, prefix behaviour predictability, adjacency/coherence, and Stage3 test_recall@10. Judgement is test_recall@10 > 0.065, not a diagnostic threshold.

risks: Co-occurrence may reflect popularity or within-user noise; rank fusion can sacrifice important reconstruction distinctions, barycentres can blur multi-interest neighbourhoods, and a single run has seed uncertainty.
ideas.safeguards: Float32 geometry/ranks even under mixed precision; clamp norms before log/exp and denominators away from zero; project every ball operation; skip empty/zero-weight rows; average exact ties and deterministic lowest-index final tie; chunk candidate distances; reject NaN/Inf with baseline-safe reconstruction-only fallback for affected items.
ideas.spec_equations: Clamp/project ball points to norm ≤(1-1e-5)/sqrt(c_abs). Karcher iteration: initialize b=exp_0(sum_j w_ij log_0(x_j)); repeat a documented fixed 5 iterations b←exp_b(sum_j w_ij log_b(x_j)); project after each update. For empty rows, set context term to tied zero ranks and use reconstruction rank only. Compute pairwise ranks by stable comparisons, assigning exact ties their average rank. Detach discrete argmin/ranks; use selected code in standard RQ-VAE straight-through/reconstruction and codebook losses. Avoid dense all-item graph materialization; cache sparse training neighbours.
ideas.spec_inputs_outputs: Inputs: batch item IDs, current encoder vectors for batch and their training neighbours, first-layer codebook vectors, frozen sparse co-occurrence rows, fixed c=-1. Output: first-layer code index per item and selected quantized vectors; later residual indices are baseline outputs.

specification.text: For item i with encoder vector z_i, let N(i),w_ij be its frozen L2-normalized co-occurrence row. Let b_i be the curvature-c=-1 Poincare Frechet barycentre of {proj(exp_0(z_j)):j in N(i)}, computed by a fixed-point Karcher iteration. For each first-level code k, let q_ik=||z_i-e_k||² and h_ik=d_P(proj(exp_0(e_k)),b_i). Set r_q(i,k)=1+#{l:q_il<q_ik}+0.5#{l!=k:q_il=q_ik}; define r_h analogously, and k*=argmin_k(r_q+r_h), ties by lowest code index. (The candidate-dependent distance is essential: d_P(z_i,b_i) alone is constant over k and cannot rank codes.)

ideas.ablation_geometry_off: Wiring check only: replace Poincare Karcher mean/distance with Euclidean weighted neighbour mean and Euclidean candidate distance; retain rank sum; never train this arm.
ideas.behavior_computation: For each user’s longest training sequence, increment each unordered distinct item pair once in both directions; L2-normalize each item’s co-occurrence row, store sparse neighbours/weights frozen before Stage 2.

ideas.cost_estimate: At 24,556 items, 24 steps/epoch and 3000 epochs (72,000 steps), each level adds B×K curved distances and rank computation plus sparse neighbour-context aggregation; for L levels this is about L times the per-level candidate scoring overhead, with context aggregation shared across levels within a step. ideas.coupling_path: Each training item’s frozen co-consumption row gathers current neighbour encoder representations into a curved context; each level’s candidate codes are ranked by curved distance to that context, and those ranks directly alter the argmin that emits that level’s SID token.

ideas.hyperbolic_operator: Fixed negative curvature c=-1 Poincare exp/log maps, weighted Karcher barycentre, and Poincare distance.
ideas.key_change: At each RQ level ℓ, form the current residual r_iℓ, compute the item’s context from the current pre-quantization encoder representations of its frozen co-occurrence neighbours, and choose among that level’s codes using reconstruction-error rank plus candidate-to-context Poincare-distance rank. ideas.leakage_boundary: Co-occurrence graph is built exclusively from training split sequences. Validation/test data and their item transitions are inaccessible to SID assignment; neighbour representations are obtained only for those training graph neighbours.
ideas.motivation: Fine-grained SID suffixes may encode collaborative distinctions that a coarse-only prefix cannot express; training co-consumption can guide each residual decision while reconstruction continues to constrain the complete code tuple.
ideas.novelty: This places the same behaviour-curved rank competition inside every sequential RQ assignment, rather than applying behaviour to only the initial region or adding an independent behaviour objective.
ideas.observables: Every level’s selected assignment and selected-code update can change; log per-level assignment differences in wiring tests, then record behaviour diagnostics and Stage3 test_recall@10. Success criterion is the frozen Stage3 test_recall@10 > 0.065.
risks: Repeated rank fusion may over-steer later residuals, where reconstruction errors are small; identical context at every level may over-count the same signal, increase compute, or destabilize residual code usage.
ideas.safeguards: Project to radius (1-1e-5)/sqrt(c_abs); clamp all denominators and atanh arguments; float32 for geometry; handle isolated items by reconstruction-only; average ties and deterministic index tie-break; finite-value fallback; sparse gather and chunked B×K×L computation.
ideas.spec_equations: For each item and level, use average rank 1+count(strictly smaller)+half count(other exact equals); minimize rank sum. Curved barycentre uses b0=exp_0(sum w log_0(x)); five fixed Karcher updates b←exp_b(sum w log_b(x)), projecting each step. Empty row means behaviour rank is a constant tie; equivalent to reconstruction-only assignment. Maintain standard residual update and STE. Complexity O(BLKd) candidate score plus sparse O(B deg d) context; chunk codes.
ideas.spec_inputs_outputs: Inputs: batch item IDs, their current encoder vectors, current encoder vectors for frozen graph neighbours, residual at each level, each level codebook, sparse weights, c=-1. Outputs: one chosen code per item per level and standard baseline quantized residual reconstruction.

specification.text: Maintain the baseline residual r_i1=z_i and candidate reconstruction errors q_iℓk=||r_iℓ-e_ℓk||². For all levels use the same frozen N(i),w_ij and current neighbour encoder vectors to obtain b_i as the c=-1 Poincare Karcher mean. Let h_iℓk=d_P(exp_0(e_ℓk),b_i); select k_iℓ=argmin_k(rank(q_iℓk)+rank(h_iℓk)) with average ranks for ties and code-index final tie-break, then r_i,ℓ+1=r_iℓ-e_ℓ,k_iℓ. The context is not built from codebook vectors or residuals.

ideas.ablation_behavior_off: Define q rows as zero and use m_i=exp_0(h_i/√d), making the behavior rank identical across codes (average tie rank); do not train this arm.
ideas.ablation_both_on: Use frozen nonzero q, current-encoder intrinsic Poincare Frechet context, hyperbolic context-distance rank plus Euclidean reconstruction rank; this is the sole candidate training run.
ideas.ablation_geometry_off: Replace exp/log, Frechet barycentre and d_-1 with Euclidean weighted mean and Euclidean distance; keep the same q and rank sum; do not train this arm.
ideas.behavior_computation: From each user's longest Stage-2 training sequence only, count every distinct item pair once, symmetrize, zero diagonal, then L2-normalize each row; freeze sparse rows before Stage 2. No validation or test sequences are read.
ideas.behavior_signal: Symmetric within-sequence item co-occurrence counts, row-L2-normalized.
ideas.cost_estimate: One Stage-2 training run only: 3000 epochs x 24 steps x four cards. Sparse context aggregation costs O(nnz(A_batch)d), with nnz bounded by the batch items' frozen neighbor lists; per layer add O(batch_size * code_count * d) hyperbolic distance and rank work, alongside baseline Euclidean code distances of the same order. Frechet iterations add O(iterations * nnz(A_batch)d); cache/reuse contexts within a step. This is an assignment-side overhead, not a second model or run.
ideas.coupling_equation: m_i=argmin_y Σ_j q_ij d_{-1}(y,exp_0(h_j/√d))²; k_i=argmin_k [rank_k ||r_i-e_k||² + rank_k d_{-1}(exp_0(h_i/√d),m_i)].
ideas.coupling_path: Frozen q_ij selects current encoder neighbor points -> their curved Frechet barycentre m_i -> curved distances from the item's representation to m_i rank candidate codes -> rank sum selects the residual code. Removing q or replacing the curved operations changes the chosen code path.

ideas.hyperbolic_location: Current pre-quantization encoder outputs are mapped to the ball for neighbor barycentres; the same context and item point enter every layer's code-assignment distance ranking.
ideas.hyperbolic_operator: Poincare ball exp/log maps, fixed-curvature (-1) distance, and intrinsic squared-distance Frechet barycentre.
ideas.key_change: Before each assignment, map current encoder outputs to a fixed-curvature Poincare ball and compute each item's co-occurrence-weighted intrinsic Frechet barycentre. ideas.leakage_boundary: A is constructed solely from the Stage-2 training split before fitting; contexts use only frozen A and current encoder outputs for training catalog items. SID generation and Stage 3 evaluation never use validation/test interactions to construct or update A or contexts.

Use q sparse row weights in a deterministic fixed iteration Frechet solver; detach barycentre result. For rank ties use average rank (1-based), then stable code-index tie break for argmin. Empty-neighbor rows use m_i=x_i, so all behavior ranks tie. specification.text: Let A_ij be the number of unordered pairs (i,j) appearing together in a user's longest Stage-2 training sequence, symmetrized, with A_ii=0; freeze q_ij=A_ij/||A_i:||_2. With curvature -c (c=1), prequantization vectors h_j are mapped to x_j=proj(exp_0(s h_j)), where s=1/sqrt(d) is a documented scale normalization. Context m_i=argmin_{y in B_c} sum_j q_ij d_c(y,x_j)^2, solved by a fixed small inner iteration of Riemannian gradient descent initialized at the weighted tangent mean exp_0(sum_j q_ij log_0(x_j)); stop-gradient through m_i to avoid second-order inner-solver gradients. At layer l, residual r_i^l and code vectors e_k^l give E_ik=||r_i^l-e_k^l||²; B_ik=d_c(exp_0(s h_i),m_i). Define ascending average ranks R_E,R_B (ties get average occupied rank); choose argmin_k R_Eik+R_Bik, smallest code index breaks exact total ties. Apply the existing straight-through quantized residual update.

ideas.title: Co-occurrence Frechet context enters rank-sum code assignment

ideas.ablation_behavior_off: Wiring switch sets \(W_{ij}=0\) for all neighbours; define the behaviour rank as tied across candidates, so selection reduces to the reconstruction ranking. Do not train this arm.
ideas.ablation_both_on: Use the frozen training-only co-occurrence rows, current-representation Poincaré barycentre, candidate-conditioned curved distances and fixed equal rank sum. Train this candidate once, for the frozen 3000 Stage 2 epochs, then run the frozen Stage 3 protocol.
ideas.ablation_geometry_off: Wiring switch replaces the Poincaré barycentre/distance/projection with Euclidean weighted mean, Euclidean distance and unconstrained addition in the same candidate-conditioned formula. Do not train this arm.
ideas.behavior_computation: Use only each user’s longest training sequence. Count every unordered pair of distinct items in that sequence once, symmetrise the resulting counts, and L2-normalise each item’s row. Freeze the sparse neighbour indices and weights before Stage 2.
ideas.behavior_signal: Symmetric item co-occurrence in users’ training sequences.
ideas.cost_estimate: Co-occurrence construction is a one-time sparse pass over training sequences. Barycentres cost \(O(\sum_i |\mathcal N_i| I)\) per assignment refresh for \(I\) fixed-point iterations; the extra candidate distances and ranks cost \(O(BK)\) per assignment step for batch size \(B\) and code count \(K\), plus sorting \(O(BK\log K)\). At the frozen scale (24 steps/epoch × 3000 epochs = 72,000 steps; 24,556 training items), the extra assignment work is repeated each step if assignments are refreshed each step; cache each item’s neighbour indices and recompute only its barycentre from current representations when that item is assigned. No extra trainable parameters are required.
ideas.coupling_equation: \(b_i=\arg\min_{b\in\mathbb B}\sum_j W_{ij}d_{-1}(b,z_j)^2;\quad q_{ik}=\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbb B}(z_i+c_k-b_i);\quad s_{ik}=r_k(\|z_i-c_k\|_2^2)+r_k(d_{-1}(q_{ik},b_i));\quad k_i=\arg\min_k s_{ik}\). Here \(W_{ij}\) is the training-behaviour term and \(d_{-1}\) is the curved term. The candidate-dependent \(q_{ik}\) ensures the behaviour/geometry rank can change the selected code.
ideas.coupling_path: Frozen training co-occurrence weights select the neighbours and weight their current encoder representations in the barycentre. That barycentre and each candidate code form \(q_{ik}\); its curved distance determines a candidate rank that is added to the reconstruction rank to select the SID.

ideas.hyperbolic_location: The barycentre is recomputed from current pre-quantisation neighbour representations during assignment; the curved distance scores each candidate’s context-conditioned point against that barycentre.
ideas.hyperbolic_operator: Poincaré-ball Fréchet barycentre and Poincaré distance at fixed negative curvature \(K=-1\), with projection onto the open unit ball.
ideas.key_change: Before Stage 2, build frozen symmetric, row-normalised co-occurrence rows from each user’s longest training sequence. During assignment, compute each item’s hyperbolic barycentre from its neighbours’ current encoder outputs, rank every candidate by Euclidean reconstruction error and by hyperbolic distance to that barycentre, and choose the code with the lowest sum of ranks.
ideas.leakage_boundary: Construct \(C\) and \(W\) exclusively from the training split before Stage 2. Do not read validation or test interactions, including for sequence selection, neighbour construction, weight normalisation, or any assignment-time context.
ideas.motivation: Items co-consumed across a user’s training history may share useful semantic structure even when their encoder representations are not nearest in Euclidean space. Letting that structure participate directly in code selection may produce SIDs whose prefixes better support next-item prediction.
ideas.novelty: The behaviour context is computed from current pre-quantisation representations of training co-occurrence neighbours, then hyperbolic proximity to that context contributes a candidate-code rank in the same assignment decision as reconstruction error. Neither the behaviour context nor the curved distance is an auxiliary loss.
ideas.observables: With both switches on, record per-item SID changes, assignment rank contributions, and behavioural coherence, adjacency and transfer-predictability diagnostics; evaluate Stage 3 test_recall@10 under the frozen protocol. A toy graph wiring check should verify that changing neighbours can change assignments, and a batch check should verify nonzero context and gradients reaching selected codes. These are checks, not trained ablation arms.
risks: Neighbour representations may be noisy early in training; a barycentre may be poorly defined for widely dispersed neighbours; the behaviour rank may override useful reconstruction choices; and the additional per-candidate curved computations may increase Stage 2 time. The stated code-conditioned point is necessary to make the hyperbolic term vary by candidate; without it the behaviour rank is constant across codes and cannot affect assignment.
ideas.safeguards: Initialise the codebook through the existing valid initialisation before the first assignment. Project encoder points and barycentre iterates inside radius \(1-\epsilon\) (for example, \(\epsilon\) derived from the dtype’s machine precision); clamp Poincaré distance arguments away from zero and the ball boundary. Use a fixed iteration/tolerance stopping rule for the barycentre, finite-value checks, and renormalise nonempty neighbour rows. Empty-neighbour items receive a tied behaviour rank and therefore use reconstruction ranking alone. Use average ranks for ties and a deterministic code-index tie-break; do not add usage balancing, Sinkhorn, tuned coupling weights, or tuned temperatures.
ideas.spec_equations: \(W_{ij}=C_{ij}/\|C_{i,:}\|_2\). If neighbours exist, \(b_i=\arg\min_b\sum_jW_{ij}d_{-1}(b,z_j)^2\); otherwise set \(r_k(h)=0\) for every code. For each candidate, \(q_{ik}=\operatorname{Proj}_{1-\epsilon}(z_i+c_k-b_i)\), \(e_{ik}=\|z_i-c_k\|^2\), \(h_{ik}=d_{-1}(q_{ik},b_i)\), \(s_{ik}=\operatorname{averageRank}_k(e_{ik})+\operatorname{averageRank}_k(h_{ik})\). Assign the smallest \(s_{ik}\), breaking residual ties by code index. Keep the existing quantizer’s reconstruction/commitment training path for the selected code.
ideas.spec_inputs_outputs: Inputs are a training item’s current encoder representation \(z_i\), current valid code vectors \(c_1,\ldots,c_K\), and its frozen sparse training co-occurrence neighbours and weights \(W_{ij}\). Output is the selected code index \(k_i\), its SID, and optional rank diagnostics.

specification.text: For training items \(i,j\), set \(C_{ij}=\sum_u \mathbf{1}[i,j\in S_u]\), counting each pair once per user’s longest training sequence; set \(W_{ij}=C_{ij}/\|C_{i,:}\|_2\) when the row is nonzero. At each assignment, let \(z_i\) be the current encoder output and \(c_k\) the valid, initialized code vectors. Compute the fixed-curvature (\(K=-1\)) Poincaré Fréchet barycentre \(b_i=\arg\min_{b\in\mathbb B}\sum_{j:W_{ij}>0}W_{ij}d_{-1}(b,z_j)^2\). For each code \(k\), compute \(e_{ik}=\|z_i-c_k\|_2^2\), \(h_{ik}=d_{-1}(z_i,b_i)\) if \(c_k\) is represented in the hyperbolic assignment space, and rank both quantities over candidate codes; choose \(k_i=\arg\min_k(r^e_{ik}+r^h_{ik})\). To make the behaviour rank code-dependent as required, use the code-conditioned point \(q_{ik}=\operatorname{Proj}_{\mathbb B}(z_i+c_k-b_i)\) and set \(h_{ik}=d_{-1}(q_{ik},b_i)\); this compares each candidate’s behaviour-context displacement rather than repeating the same distance for every code. Use ascending average ranks for ties and deterministic lowest-index tie-breaking after rank sums. The decision rule is the rank sum, which is discrete, so the mechanism also returns the differentiable scores of the same two quantities: the straight-through path of the quantiser carries the gradient of the Euclidean and hyperbolic distances, while the hard choice stays the rank sum with the lowest index breaking a tie. This is the only reading of the mechanism in which the behaviour signal trains the encoder and the codebook instead of only relabelling codes.

ideas.ablation_behavior_off: Wiring-only switch: set the behaviour rank to zero for every code, leaving the Euclidean reconstruction assignment. Do not train this arm.
ideas.ablation_both_on: The sole trained candidate uses training co-occurrence weights, curvature -1 Frechet contexts and hyperbolic-distance ranks, summed with Euclidean reconstruction ranks. No off-arm is trained.
ideas.ablation_geometry_off: Wiring-only switch: use Euclidean weighted mean of the same live neighbor encoder outputs and Euclidean distance for the context rank (retain the reconstruction rank). Do not train this arm.
ideas.behavior_computation: On each user's longest Stage2 training sequence, count every unordered pair of distinct items once; symmetrize counts, then L2-normalize each item row. ideas.cost_estimate: Baseline budget is 24,556 items x 24 steps/epoch x 3,000 epochs = 1,768,032,000 item-step assignments across four cards. ideas.coupling_path: Frozen neighbours and weights -> current neighbor encoder outputs -> hyperbolic Frechet context -> per-code hyperbolic distance ranks -> rank-sum with each code's Euclidean reconstruction-error rank -> selected code and existing straight-through training update. Behaviour-off removes the context rank; geometry-off replaces barycentre/distance with Euclidean weighted mean/distance.

Context gradients flow through neighbor representations and selected-code straight-through path; sparse graph weights are constants. specification.text: For each item i, let N_i,w_ij be nonzero entries of its L2-normalized symmetric co-occurrence row. For current residual input x_i and code c_k, e_ik=||x_i-c_k||_2^2 and h_ik=d_B(phi(x_i),b_i). Let r^e_ik=1+#{l:e_il<e_ik}+0.5*#{l!=k:e_il=e_ik}; define r^h analogously. k*=argmin_k(r^e_ik+r^h_ik), ties by lower code index. The rank coefficients are fixed at one; this is not a tuned coupling weight. Empty N_i uses behaviour rank zero for every k (equivalently omit its contribution), leaving the baseline reconstruction argmin.

objective:
Discover new mechanisms in which TRAINING-ONLY user behaviour and HYPERBOLIC geometry are computationally coupled to improve the RQ-VAE Semantic IDs used by a generative next-item recommender, with the real target of Stage3 test Recall@10 above 0.065.

## The direction of this round: the co-occurrence behaviour of the training sequences participates directly in the hyperbolic code assignment

One direction only. The co-occurrence behaviour of the training sequences must decide which
semantic ID a product gets, together with the hyperbolic geometry, **on the same code-assignment
path**. Not a behaviour score that is computed and then discarded, and not a context taken from
a zero-initialised codebook.

### The mechanism, in full

1. **The behaviour signal** is the symmetric co-occurrence of the training sequences only: for
   each user's longest training sequence, every pair of items inside it co-occurs once, and the
   per-item co-occurrence rows are L2-normalised. The co-occurrence neighbours and their weights
   are frozen before Stage 2. No validation or test behaviour, no future information.

2. **The behaviour context** of an item is the hyperbolic barycentre (fixed negative curvature)
   of the **pre-quantisation representations of its co-occurrence neighbours** - the encoder
   output of those neighbours, not the codebook vectors. The codebook must hold valid values
   before the first assignment, through the existing initialisation, and the context must be
   recomputed from the current representations as they move.

3. **The assignment** compares every candidate code on two quantities and combines them by
   **rank**:
   * the Euclidean reconstruction error the code would cause for this item, and
   * the hyperbolic distance between the item's representation and the behaviour context.

   Each quantity is turned into the **rank of the code among the candidates** and the two ranks
   are added; the code with the lowest total rank wins. A code that reconstructs best and sits
   fifth from the behaviour context scores 1+5=6; another that ranks third and first scores
   3+1=4, so the second code is chosen. The rank combination is a **fixed design choice** (each
   of the two terms counts once), stated in advance, not a weight that was found by trying
   values. It removes the coupling weight, the clip bound and the temperature from the
   mechanism, because there is no constant left to tune.

### What this round must not do

* **No Sinkhorn and no balancing of the code usage.** It needs a regularisation strength or a
  target usage distribution of its own, forcing uniform usage does not fit long-tail data, it
  cannot guarantee that the mechanism avoids a collapse, and it would make a single run harder
  to read. The reconstruction term and the rank combination have to carry the mechanism.
* **No ablation arm, no constant sweep, no seed repetition.** The behaviour switch, the
  curvature switch and the both-on path stay in the code, and the cheap wiring checks are
  welcome: changing a toy co-occurrence graph changes the code assignment, the curved distance
  really enters the assignment score, and the context of a real training batch is non-zero with
  a gradient that reaches the selected code. That is all: one candidate, one Stage 2 run, one
  frozen Stage 3 evaluation. The behavioural diagnostics are recorded, never used as an admission
  gate; the Stage 3 `test_recall@10` is the judgement.

### What the earlier arms do and do not show

`TIGER_incoming_context_barycenter` reached `test_recall@10` about 0.0585.
`TIGER_cogeo_region_argmax` reached 0.0398, but it did not use the co-occurrence signal in the
assignment at all and took its context from a zero-initialised codebook, so its low recall is
**not** a valid test of "co-occurrence context plus hyperbolic geometry". This round puts the
weight on the one question that is still open: **does the context really enter the code
assignment**, and what does the mechanism do when it does.

## Requirements for the proposal

* the equations of the mechanism, the two ranks and their combination, the inputs and outputs;
* where the curvature acts (the barycentre and the distance), and where the behaviour acts
  (the neighbours and their weights);
* the numerical safeguards (the ball boundary, the rank computation with ties, the degenerate
  case of an item without neighbours);
* the training cost, and the three switches (behaviour off, geometry off, both on) defined but
  not trained;
* what should observably change, and how the mechanism would be judged: the Stage 3
  `test_recall@10`, with the behavioural diagnostics recorded alongside.

## Frozen constraints

Four tokens, 3000 Stage 2 epochs on four cards, no early stopping, the frozen Stage 3 protocol,
the baseline is `stage2_RQ-VAE/TIGER_RQ-VAE` and every candidate is a fresh copy of it.

It is widely employed in tokenizing data representations for large language models, diffusion models, and other generative models. Despite its prevalence, the characteristics and behaviors of vector quantization in generative models remain largely underexplored. In this study, we investigate representation collapse in vector quantization - a critical degradation where codebook tokens or latent embeddings lose their discriminative power by converging to a limited subset of values. This collapse fundamentally compromises the model's ability to capture diverse data patterns. By leveraging both synthetic and real datasets, we identify the severity of each type of collapses and triggering conditions. Our analysis reveals that restricted initialization and limited encoder capacity result in tokens collapse and embeddings collapse. Building on these findings, we propose potential solutions aimed at mitigating each collapse. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive study examining representation collapsing problems in vector quantization.
papers.title: Representation Collapsing Problems in Vector Quantization

papers.abstract: Machine learning algorithms have been shown to be highly effective in solving optimization problems in a wide range of applications. Such algorithms typically use gradient descent with backpropagation and the chain rule. Hence, the backpropagation fails if intermediate gradients are zero for some functions in the computational graph, because it causes the gradients to collapse when multiplying with zero. Vector quantization is one of those challenging functions for machine learning algorithms, since it is a piece-wise constant function and its gradient is zero almost everywhere. A typical solution is to apply the straight through estimator which simply copies the gradients over the vector quantization function in the backpropagation. Other solutions are based on smooth or stochastic approximation. This study proposes a vector quantization technique called NSVQ, which approximates the vector quantization behavior by substituting a multiplicative noise so that it can be used for machine learning problems. Specifically, the vector quantization error is replaced by product of the original error and a normalized noise vector, the samples of which are drawn from a zero-mean, unit-varianc

findings.detail: The code has a connected behaviour-and-curvature assignment path, but it does not implement the specified mechanism. The context is an origin-tangent log-map weighted mean followed by projection, not the specified Poincaré Fréchet barycentre minimizer. More importantly, candidate behaviour ranks compare each code centroid to the item context; the specification requires the candidate-conditioned point q_ik = Proj(z_i + c_k - b_i) and its distance to b_i. The stated co-occurrence normalization is also L1 (line 289), rather than the specified row L2 normalization. Thus the implemented mechanism is not faithful to COOC_RANK_FRECHET as specified.

findings.detail: The trainer computes the score-producing latent under `torch.no_grad()`, and the refreshed centroid/context are also computed under `torch.no_grad()`. The added soft assignment term can carry gradients to the codebook, but it is not a differentiable coupled behaviour/geometry term reaching the encoder. The supplied smoke test does not establish the required switch comparisons: it checks that distances differ and that a codebook gradient is nonzero, but does not check assignments or gradients changing under behaviour-off and geometry-off; its “different graph” case also uses newly sampled embeddings for the second context (smoke_test.py:57-60, 81-85), confounding that comparison.
findings.reproduction: In the trainer’s batch path, inspect `with torch.no_grad()` around `raw_module.encoder(batch)` at lines 503-504, then follow `assignment_scores` into the detached-code soft distribution at model/layers.py:145-147. The score computation has no encoder gradient path. In smoke_test.py, compare lines 57-60 with 81-85: each context is computed from a different random embedding tensor.

findings.detail: The implemented behaviour signal does not match the specified co-occurrence rows. findings.correction: Make the intended differentiable coupled contribution explicit if encoder gradients from the mechanism are required, while retaining hard rank assignment for SID choice if desired. findings.detail: The trainer calculates assignment scores under torch.no_grad() using a separately computed encoder output. findings.correction: Compute the specified barycentre with a numerically safeguarded fixed-point minimisation of the weighted squared Poincaré distances. For each item and candidate, form and project `q_ik = z_i + c_k - b_i`, then rank `d(q_ik,b_i)` alongside the Euclidean reconstruction error. Keep the behaviour-off and geometry-off modes as explicit controls.
findings.detail: The implementation does not implement the specified Poincaré Fréchet barycentre or code-conditioned candidate point. It instead averages neighbours’ log-map vectors and projects the result (a tangent-space mean approximation), then ranks each code centroid by its distance to that context. The proposed assignment explicitly requires \(b_i=\arg\min_b\sum_j W_{ij}d(b,z_j)^2\) and \(q_{ik}=\operatorname{Proj}(z_i+c_k-b_i)\), with candidate distance \(d(q_{ik},b_i)\). Thus the exercised path is behaviour–geometry coupled, but it is a materially different mechanism from the submitted idea.
findings.reproduction: Inspect `refresh_behaviour_state` at lines 330-334: no Fréchet objective or iterative minimisation is performed. Inspect `behaviour_distances` at lines 368-376: distances are from `context` to `centroid`; no item latent `z` or candidate-conditioned `q_ik` is used.

findings.correction: Because this mechanism acts through discrete code assignment, explicitly test selected assignments under both-on, behaviour-off, and geometry-off fixtures chosen to distinguish them; do not claim differentiability of the rank operation. Separately verify finite training loss and gradients to the intended trainable model/codebook parameters through the real trainer path. Implement the corrected candidate-conditioned geometry from check (a) before validating its effect.
findings.detail: The smoke test does not establish the required switch-dependent assignment or gradient behaviour. The training assignment uses hard nested `argsort` ranks, so the rank-sum score has no gradient to `centroid`, `context`, or the encoder latent used to form the scores. The test’s nonzero codebook gradient can come from the ordinary quantization/reconstruction loss and therefore does not show that the coupled term is live. More importantly, its curved-versus-flat assertion only checks that distance values differ; it never checks that assignments or gradients change and change back across all three modes.
findings.reproduction: In `smoke_test.py:88-96`, replace the coupled scores with any detached assignment scores while retaining the model loss: the test’s codebook-gradient assertion can still be satisfied by the standard model loss. `smoke_test.py:72-75` checks only `allclose` on distance tensors, not mode-dependent selected codes or gradients.

findings.correction: If the mechanism is intended to train encoder parameters through the coupled term, compute the scoring latent and code-dependent score inputs with gradients enabled and ensure the coupled score contribution is differentiable; keep any discrete ranking/assignment operation separate as needed. Extend the one-run gradient smoke to verify the intended parameter gradients and switch-dependent behavior, without training ablation arms.
findings.detail: The score-producing encoder call is under `torch.no_grad()`, and the code vectors supplied to scoring are detached. Thus the coupled score and its soft candidate distribution have no gradient path to the encoder or through the curved behaviour computation. The soft term can reach the codebook, but the intended behaviour-conditioned curved mechanism does not update the encoder through that path. The smoke test only asserts a nonzero codebook gradient; it does not check encoder gradients or switch-dependent gradients.
findings.reproduction: In the real batch path, retain gradients on the encoder output and inspect its gradient attributable to the assignment-score soft term: it is absent because `latent` is computed under `no_grad` and scores depend on detached codes. The smoke test’s codebook-only assertion at `smoke_test.py:95-96` passes without detecting this.

findings.correction: Use a numerically stable Poincaré distance implementation, such as the equivalent `2 / sqrt(curvature) * asinh(sqrt(curvature * delta / denominator))`, with finite safeguards for the denominator; alternatively ensure the argument floor is large enough that `1 + argument` is representably greater than 1 in the input dtype and verify finite gradients at coincident points.
findings.detail: The hyperbolic distance can produce an infinite or NaN gradient in float32 when the conditioned point equals the context, or is sufficiently close. In that case `argument` is clamped to `1e-12`, but `1.0 + argument` can round to exactly `1.0` in float32. `acosh` has an unbounded derivative at 1, so the backward path through the behavior score is numerically unstable. This undermines the required finite-gradient training path.
findings.reproduction: Call `behaviour_distance` with float32 tensors where `conditioned == context_point` (for example, zero encoded and context vectors with a zero code vector), then backpropagate the sum of the returned distances. The distance’s `acosh(1.0 + argument)` can evaluate at 1.0 and yield non-finite gradients.

findings.correction: Implement the Poincaré log map with the tangent direction from `base` to `point` (for example, use `(-base) ⊕ point` in the Mobius difference), then verify that a one-point weighted mean returns that point and that a multi-point iteration remains finite and moves toward its neighbours. findings.detail: `ball_log_map(base, point)` computes `ball_add(base, -point)`, which points from `point` toward `base`, rather than the tangent from `base` toward `point`. `frechet_mean` then averages those reversed vectors and applies them with `ball_exp_map`, moving its estimate away from the neighbours instead of toward them. This makes the context used in the coupled ranking an incorrect barycentre and can drive the iteration toward the ball boundary; the current clamps can conceal that divergence rather than correct it.
findings.reproduction: Take a one-dimensional ball point `base=0` and a neighbour `point=a` for any nonzero `0 < a < 1`. The implemented log map returns a negative tangent, and the exp-map update moves the estimate below zero—away from `a`. With a single positive-weight neighbour, a Fréchet mean should return that neighbour.

findings.correction: Compute the logarithm displacement as `ball_add(-base, point, curvature)` and use an exponential map with the correct base-point conformal factor. findings.detail: `ball_log_map(base, point)` computes `ball_add(base, -point)`. The Poincaré logarithm from `base` to `point` requires the displacement `(-base) ⊕ point`; this implementation instead uses `base ⊕ (-point)`, reversing the displacement at the origin and using the wrong displacement away from it. `frechet_mean` at lines 69-72 adds that incorrect tangent step to the estimate, so the alleged Fréchet iteration moves in the wrong direction. For example, with a one-dimensional estimate at 0 and a neighbour at 0.2, the computed tangent is negative, and the update moves away from the neighbour. Thus the behaviour context does not implement the specified hyperbolic barycentre.
findings.reproduction: On a one-dimensional ball, evaluate `ball_log_map(torch.tensor([[0.]]), torch.tensor([[0.2]]), 1.0)`: the result is negative, although the tangent from the origin toward the positive point must be positive. Then call `frechet_mean` on a single point at 0.2 with weight 1; its update moves away rather than toward that point.

findings.correction: Implement the Poincaré log map using `(-base) ⊕ point` and the correct conformal factor at the base; implement the exp map with the base conformal factor in its tangent scaling. findings.detail: The purported Riemannian log and exp maps omit required operations, so the neighbour barycentre iteration is not the specified Poincaré Fréchet mean. `ball_log_map` computes `base ⊕ (-point)` rather than `(-base) ⊕ point`, reversing the displacement for non-origin bases. `ball_exp_map` applies the tangent step without the base-point conformal factor. Consequently `refresh_behaviour_state` iterates using an incorrect tangent displacement and update; the curved behaviour context and resulting assignment ranks do not faithfully implement the proposed barycentre mechanism. This is a correctness issue in the core coupling, not a demand for an ablation or a quality threshold.
findings.reproduction: Use a nonzero base and a distinct point in `ball_log_map(base, point)`: its displacement points according to `base ⊕ (-point)`, not the logarithmic displacement from base to point. Then apply `ball_exp_map` to that result at the same base; the omitted base conformal factor means it does not implement the corresponding Riemannian exponential update. The barycentre loop at train_rqvae.py:317-323 uses these operations directly.

findings.correction: Compute average ranks for ties with tensor operations on the device, or another vectorized ranking implementation that avoids per-row `.tolist()` and Python loops. Preserve ascending average ranks and deterministic lowest-index tie-breaking.
findings.detail: Tie handling copies the sorted values to CPU with `.tolist()` and then performs Python-level per-code comparisons for every batch row. With 1,024 items per rank and 256 candidates, this processes about 262,000 Python comparisons for each rank calculation, twice per training step. findings.correction: Implement the Poincaré exponential-map scale with the base-point conformal factor, preserving the existing small-norm and ball-projection safeguards; then verify exp/log recovery for nonzero bases and confirm the context refresh uses that corrected map. findings.detail: `ball_exp_map` omits the Poincaré conformal factor at the base point. For curvature \(c\), the exponential map’s tangent scaling depends on \(\lambda_x=2/(1-c\|x\|^2)\); the implemented scaling is only `tanh(sqrt(c)*norm/2)/(sqrt(c)*norm)`. Consequently, the eight-step iteration called as the Fréchet barycentre in `train_rqvae.py:317-324` does not perform the specified Riemannian update except at the origin. This undermines the proposal’s curved behaviour context and makes the geometry-off comparison unreliable as a test of that mechanism.
findings.reproduction: Use two distinct points in the unit Poincaré ball with a nonzero base point, compute `ball_exp_map(base, tangent, 1.0)`, then compute `ball_log_map(base, result, 1.0)`. The result will not recover the input tangent in general; the discrepancy grows away from the origin. This breaks the exp/log inverse required by the barycentre iteration.
